tagline.text: A triangular city park among the towers of Makati

location.label: Location
location.text: Makati Central Business District (between Paseo de Roxas, Makati Avenue and Ayala Avenue)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0~800 (per person, free entry; including a café or meal)

children.text: A triangular city park of about 2 hectares in the middle of the Makati Central Business District. Entry is free, and you can stroll, jog or eat outdoors, and it is also known for the Festival of Lights that starts in November.

Ayala Triangle Gardens is a triangular city park in the heart of the Makati Central Business District (CBD) in Metro Manila. It is surrounded by three roads, Paseo de Roxas, Makati Avenue and Ayala Avenue, and covers about 2 hectares (about 20,000 sq m). It opened to the public in November 2009 and is run by the developer Ayala Land. It is said to have been inspired by London's Hyde Park. It counts among the largest green spaces in Makati, and it is not easy to find such an open lawn in an area packed with offices and malls.

The land was once Nielson Field, Manila's airport before World War II. The airport closed in 1948 and moved to the site of today's Ninoy Aquino International Airport, after which the Ayala family developed the area as a commercial district, and the old runways became the roads that now surround the park. The old control tower was preserved and is used as a restaurant today. In the 1980s the site also hosted protests against the Marcos dictatorship.

More than 100 trees, including rain trees, golden palms and fire trees, shade the park, and lawns, walking paths, public art and memorials are scattered throughout. The Ninoy Aquino monument, erected in 1986, stands at the northwest corner, and the McMicking memorial and water feature, lit up at night, are also worth a look. Entry is free, so it is a good place to take a short break while shopping or working in Makati.
It is not a major sightseeing destination. Think of it as a rest stop to fit between Makati city plans rather than the centerpiece of a day. During the
Festival of Lights

, which runs from November to the following January, the evening hours are the best time to visit, and early on Sunday mornings the surrounding roads are closed to traffic and fill with people running and exercising. It is known among Korean visitors in the Philippines as a spot to walk and have a coffee after lunch while working or shopping in Makati, and it is often combined with a visit to Greenbelt. The park is ringed by buildings such as Ayala Tower One, the Makati Stock Exchange building, Nielson Tower, Ayala Triangle Tower One and Two and the Mandarin Oriental Manila, so you can take in the skyline of Makati's financial district at a glance. There is also news that a 3x3 basketball court and pickleball courts were added to the Sunday car-free area in 2025, so check on site how to use them.

blocks.title: Green space and walking paths in the city

children.text: Paths for walking and jogging run between lawns and shade trees surrounded by high-rise buildings. It is a good place to escape Makati's heat and noise for a while. In the morning you often see local residents running and doing yoga, and at lunchtime office workers out with a packed lunch or coffee.

blocks.title: A festival of light and sound

children.text: Every year from November to the following January, a Christmas-themed light and sound show is held. Performances run at intervals of about
30 minutes
from
6 PM
to
10 PM
, and viewing is free. The schedule changes each year, so check the latest announcement.
The park area was the site of Nielson Field airport before the war. The control tower from that era was preserved and is now the restaurant Blackbird, a good way to feel Makati's history.

The Ninoy Aquino monument, erected in 1986, stands at the northwest corner. Monuments honoring Gabriela Silang and Muhammad Kudarat also stand at corners of the park, so you can trace a bit of Philippine history.
Public art by Filipino artists is installed here, and the McMicking memorial and water feature are lit at night, changing the mood. There are several good spots to take photos along the walk.

Outdoor restaurants cluster behind the Makati Stock Exchange building, and there are also restaurants and a food court inside Ayala Triangle Tower. You can rest in the park and eat in one trip. Shops and opening hours can change, so check before you go.
Since September 2023, the roads around the park, including Ayala Avenue, have been closed on Sunday mornings from
6 AM
to
10 AM
. During these hours the roads become walking, running and cycling routes, and you can see a very different Makati.
Enter the park from the Ayala Avenue side and walk once around the edge path. Plenty of tree shade makes it relatively comfortable even by day.
Look around the Ninoy Aquino monument, the public art works and the McMicking memorial area.
Rest on the lawn or a bench and take photos.
Have lunch at an outdoor restaurant behind the park or at a restaurant in Ayala Triangle Tower.

The park itself does not take long to circle. It is better to plan your day around a meal or nearby attractions. If it is a Sunday morning, also walk the roads around the park during the car-free event hours.
Arrive around sunset and have dinner at a nearby restaurant while checking out a spot.
Enter the park in time for the first show. Shows run at intervals of about 30 minutes.
Watch one round before it gets crowded, then stroll the memorial area lit up for the night.
Walk to Greenbelt and finish with shopping or coffee.
On weekend evenings during the Festival of Lights it is very crowded. Early on a weekday is recommended.

items.title: From the Manila airport and city

children.text: From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to central Makati, a taxi or Grab is the simplest way. Travel time varies widely with traffic, so allow plenty of time.
From central Manila (Ermita, Malate and so on), take a taxi or Grab and ask for Ayala Avenue or Paseo de Roxas.
Give the destination as Ayala Triangle or Ayala Tower One rather than the park name, which makes it easier for drivers to understand.

Get off at MRT-3 Ayala Station, enter One Ayala and walk through the connected malls, which takes about 7 to 10 minutes (2026 guide). You can also take a jeepney or bus along Ayala Avenue to the Paseo de Roxas intersection.
If you ride the EDSA Carousel bus, get off at One Ayala and walk as described above. Routes and stops can change, so check on site.
You can walk between Greenbelt or Ayala Center and the park through underpasses and walkways.
Several city bus routes are said to stop at the Ayala Triangle stop in front of the park. Routes can change, so check on site.

As an outdoor park, it is best visited in the cooler dry season. The sun is strong at midday, so early morning or around sunset is recommended. One guide names the time before 9 AM as the least crowded.

From November to the following January the Festival of Lights runs, making evenings the most spectacular. From 6 AM to 10 AM on Sundays the surrounding roads are closed to traffic, which is good for exercise. In the June to November rainy season, sudden downpours are common and the lawns can get wet, so on rainy days plan indoor activities connected to the malls.

Right next to the park there are upscale hotels such as the Mandarin Oriental Manila, and the Makati CBD has hotels in a range of price levels. When choosing a place to stay, consider access to nearby malls and rail stations along your route as well as the park. Makati has many business travelers, so weekday rates are often higher than weekend rates; compare by date. Staying at a hotel near the park makes it easy to get to a morning jog or the Sunday morning car-free event.

Outdoor restaurants cluster behind the park, and there are restaurants and a food court inside Ayala Triangle Tower. Blackbird, in the old control tower, is known as a place for special occasions with a nice atmosphere, but check reservations and prices in advance. Greenbelt and Ayala Center, within walking distance, have even more choices. There are also many Korean and Japanese restaurants and cafés in central Makati, so if you miss Korean food you can easily find it along your route. Restaurants at lunchtime fill with office workers, so it is better to avoid right after 12 noon.
The park is generally listed as open from 6 AM to 10 PM, so check the latest announcement before you visit.
Midday is very hot. Go early in the morning or around sunset and bring water.
During the Festival of Lights, it is better to arrive before the first show and get a spot; weekend evenings are very crowded.
On Sunday mornings the surrounding roads are closed, so if you plan to travel by car, check a detour route.
Grab is convenient for getting around Makati. At rush hour fares go up and cars are hard to get.
Guidance says pets are allowed only on a leash. Cleaning up after them is a must.
Park rules are listed as prohibiting alcohol, smoking, glass bottles and skateboards.
Free Wi-Fi is mentioned in the park, but speed and availability may not be consistent, so also bring mobile data.
Makati's underpasses and walkways are well connected; if you are unsure of the way, ask at an information sign or a security guard.
Under park rules, you must not pick or damage plants, and you must take your trash with you or put it in designated places.
Crowds gather during festivals and events. In 2017 a concert was cancelled midway because of overcrowding, so take care of your belongings and your group.
Pickpocketing and phone snatching are common in crowded busy areas. Carry your bag in front of you.
Nearby buildings such as Ayala Tower One have strict security and require ID and a reason for the visit. Photographing the exterior is allowed.
In the rainy season sudden showers fall. Carry an umbrella or raincoat.
Holding gatherings or events in the park without permission is listed as prohibited.
Hours and rules can change, so check on-site notices and Ayala Land announcements.
A shopping and dining complex within walking distance of the park. Good for continuing with shopping or a meal.
You can explore the whole Makati Central Business District where the park sits, taking in malls, museums and dining areas together.
A weekend market held at Salcedo Park in Salcedo Village from
7 AM
to
2 PM
on Saturdays. Worth stopping by together on a Saturday visit.
A market held on Sunday mornings at Legazpi Active Park in San Lorenzo Village. You can fit it into a Sunday morning plan.
